claim: Lower vertebrate and neonatal mammalian hearts exhibit the capacity to regenerate through the reprogramming of pre-existing cardiomyocytes.
source: Lower vertebrate and neonatal mammalian hearts exhibit the remarkable capacity to regenerate through the reprogramming of pre-existing cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about cardiac regeneration capacity.

claim: Altered hemodynamic forces due to cardiac injury activate a sequential endocardial-myocardial signaling cascade to direct cardiomyocyte reprogramming and heart regeneration.
source: Here, we utilize in vivo biophysical and genetic fate mapping zebrafish studies to reveal that altered hemodynamic forces due to cardiac injury activate a sequential endocardial-myocardial signaling cascade to direct cardiomyocyte reprogramming and heart regeneration.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study as stated in the abstract, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Altered hemodynamic forces are sensed by the endocardium through the mechanosensitive channel Trpv4.
source: Specifically, these altered forces are sensed by the endocardium through the mechanosensitive channel Trpv4 to control Klf2a transcription factor expression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data using trpv4 mutants shown in Figure 5.

claim: Trpv4 controls Klf2a transcription factor expression in the endocardium.
source: Specifically, these altered forces are sensed by the endocardium through the mechanosensitive channel Trpv4 to control Klf2a transcription factor expression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5 showing reduced klf2a expression in trpv4 mutants.

claim: Klf2a activates endocardial Notch signaling.
source: Consequently, Klf2a then activates endocardial Notch signaling which results in the non-cell autonomous initiation of myocardial Erbb2 and BMP signaling to promote cardiomyocyte reprogramming and heart regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5 showing reduced Notch signaling in klf2a mutants.

claim: Endocardial Notch signaling initiates myocardial Erbb2 signaling non-cell autonomously.
source: Consequently, Klf2a then activates endocardial Notch signaling which results in the non-cell autonomous initiation of myocardial Erbb2 and BMP signaling to promote cardiomyocyte reprogramming and heart regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7 showing reduced Erbb2 pathway components after Notch inhibition.

claim: Endocardial Notch signaling initiates myocardial BMP signaling non-cell autonomously.
source: Consequently, Klf2a then activates endocardial Notch signaling which results in the non-cell autonomous initiation of myocardial Erbb2 and BMP signaling to promote cardiomyocyte reprogramming and heart regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7 showing reduced BMP signaling after Notch inhibition.

claim: Myocardial Erbb2 and BMP signaling promote cardiomyocyte reprogramming and heart regeneration.
source: Consequently, Klf2a then activates endocardial Notch signaling which results in the non-cell autonomous initiation of myocardial Erbb2 and BMP signaling to promote cardiomyocyte reprogramming and heart regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6 showing reduced cardiomyocyte proliferation and regeneration after BMP and Erbb2 inhibition.

claim: Neonatal mammalian hearts can regenerate through cardiomyocyte de-differentiation and proliferation.
source: In mammals, this reprogramming can lead to CM de-differentiation by activating cardiac developmental transcription factors to adaptively create more CMs for regenerating neonatal hearts via proliferation (Porrello et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Porrello et al., 2011.

claim: Zebrafish ventricular cardiomyocytes can de-differentiate to produce more cardiomyocytes during heart regeneration.
source: Moreover, while zebrafish ventricular CMs can de-differentiate to produce more of these CMs during heart regeneration in a manner similar to neonatal mammalian hearts (Jopling et al., 2010; Kikuchi et al., 2010), zebrafish atrial CMs also retain sufficient plasticity to trans-differentiate in order to create new ventricular CMs for regenerating cardiac ventricles (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Jopling et al., 2010 and Kikuchi et al., 2010.

claim: Zebrafish atrial cardiomyocytes can trans-differentiate to create new ventricular cardiomyocytes for regenerating cardiac ventricles.
source: Moreover, while zebrafish ventricular CMs can de-differentiate to produce more of these CMs during heart regeneration in a manner similar to neonatal mammalian hearts (Jopling et al., 2010; Kikuchi et al., 2010), zebrafish atrial CMs also retain sufficient plasticity to trans-differentiate in order to create new ventricular CMs for regenerating cardiac ventricles (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013, and further confirmed by lineage tracing experiments in Figure 1.

claim: Notch, BMP and Erbb2 signaling participate in modulating heart regeneration.
source: Although several signaling cues including Notch, BMP and Erbb2 participate in modulating heart regeneration (D'Uva et al., 2015; Gemberling et al., 2015; Mahmoud et al., 2015; Münch et al., 2017; Polizzotti et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2016; Xiang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2014), how cardiac injury activates these pathways to initiate CM reprogramming and heart regeneration remains to be elucidated.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Biomechanical forces generated by blood flow can contribute to heart development through modulating Notch, BMP and Erbb2 signaling pathways.
source: Recent studies have revealed that biomechanical forces generated by blood flow can contribute significantly to heart development through modulating Notch, BMP and Erbb2 signaling pathways (Dietrich et al., 2014; Goddard et al., 2017; Heckel et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016; Peshkovsky et al., 2011; Rasouli and Stainier, 2017; Samsa et al., 2015; Steed et al., 2016; Vermot et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Hemodynamic forces activate the endocardial flow-sensitive transcription factor Klf2 during cardiac valve development.
source: During mammalian and zebrafish cardiac valve development, hemodynamic forces activate the endocardial flow-sensitive transcription factor Klf2 as well as Notch signaling to sculpt the atrio-ventricular valve (Goddard et al., 2017; Heckel et al., 2015; Steed et al., 2016; Vermot et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Hemodynamic forces activate Notch signaling during cardiac valve development.
source: During mammalian and zebrafish cardiac valve development, hemodynamic forces activate the endocardial flow-sensitive transcription factor Klf2 as well as Notch signaling to sculpt the atrio-ventricular valve (Goddard et al., 2017; Heckel et al., 2015; Steed et al., 2016; Vermot et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Hemodynamic forces regulate endocardial Notch signaling and myocardial Erbb2 signaling to promote cardiomyocyte proliferation and migration during cardiac trabeculation.
source: Additionally, these forces regulate not only endocardial Notch signaling but also myocardial Erbb2 signaling to promote the proliferation and migration of CMs during cardiac trabeculation (Lee et al., 2016; Peshkovsky et al., 2011; Rasouli and Stainier, 2017; Samsa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: MTZ treatment of vmhc:mCherry-NTR zebrafish results in extensive cardiomyocyte death within the ventricle.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Zhang et al., 2013), MTZ treatment results initially in extensive CM death within the ventricle as detected by TUNEL staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), and then a subsequent CM proliferative response in both ventricle and atrium as detected by both phospho-histone H3 studies and EdU staining (Figure 1A–E,L–P, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: MTZ treatment of vmhc:mCherry-NTR zebrafish results in a subsequent cardiomyocyte proliferative response in both ventricle and atrium.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Zhang et al., 2013), MTZ treatment results initially in extensive CM death within the ventricle as detected by TUNEL staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), and then a subsequent CM proliferative response in both ventricle and atrium as detected by both phospho-histone H3 studies and EdU staining (Figure 1A–E,L–P, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by phospho-histone H3 and EdU staining data shown in Figure 1A-E, L-P and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Cardiomyocyte proliferation after ventricular ablation leads to recovery of both ventricular tissue and contractile function at 96 hr post-MTZ treatment.
source: As a result, this CM proliferation leads to recovery of both ventricular tissue and contractile function at 96 hr post-MTZ treatment (hpt) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by ventricular area and fractional area change measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: Differentiated atrial cardiomyocytes cannot contribute to uninjured hearts at 5 dpf.
source: Moreover, while differentiated atrial CMs cannot contribute to uninjured hearts at this stage (Foglia et al., 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), they do trans-differentiate into new ventricular CMs which help to recover the injured ventricle as previously reported (Zhang et al., 2013) (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lineage tracing data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citation to Foglia et al., 2016.

claim: Differentiated atrial cardiomyocytes trans-differentiate into new ventricular cardiomyocytes to help recover the injured ventricle.
source: Moreover, while differentiated atrial CMs cannot contribute to uninjured hearts at this stage (Foglia et al., 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), they do trans-differentiate into new ventricular CMs which help to recover the injured ventricle as previously reported (Zhang et al., 2013) (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lineage tracing data in Figure 1G,H and citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Tp1:eGFP Notch reporter signaling activity is elevated throughout vmhc:mCherry-NTR ventricle-ablated hearts.
source: In line with previous Notch signaling studies during cardiac regeneration (Zhang et al., 2013), we discovered elevated Tp1:eGFP Notch reporter signaling activity throughout these vmhc:mCherry-NTR ventricle-ablated hearts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Endocardial Notch activity is specifically elevated in the endocardium within the AVC and its surrounding atrial and ventricular regions after ventricular injury.
source: We observed that endocardial Notch activity is specifically elevated in the endocardium within the AVC and its surrounding atrial and ventricular regions but reduced furthest away from the AVC (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Tp1:d2GFP imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: notch1b is expressed in a similar pattern to Tp1:d2GFP in ventricle-injured hearts.
source: Confirming these findings, we also detected by in situ hybridization that notch1b is also expressed in a similar pattern in ventricle-injured hearts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E,F.

claim: Injury-induced endocardial Notch activity peaks at 24 hpt but diminishes as the heart regenerates.
source: Moreover, this injury-induced endocardial Notch activity peaks at 24 hpt but diminishes as the heart regenerates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by time-course Tp1:d2GFP quantitation in Figure 1—figure supplement 3G.

claim: By 96 hpt, Notch activity in ablated hearts returns to levels similar to control hearts.
source: By 96 hpt, this Notch activity in the ablated hearts returns to levels similarly observed in control hearts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G) and correlates to when ventricular tissue and contractility have recovered (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Tp1:d2GFP quantitation in Figure 1—figure supplement 3G.

claim: Global dnMAML Notch inhibition prevents cardiomyocytes from proliferating in injured hearts.
source: Confocal microscopy imaging of heat-shocked/HS (A, B, L, M) vmhc:mCherry-NTR, (C, D) vmhc:mCherry-NTR; hsp70l:dnM and (N, O) vmhc:mCherry-NTR; kdrl:Cre; hsp70l:RS-dnM hearts reveals that (D) global or (O) endocardial-specific dnMAML (dnM) Notch inhibition inhibits CM proliferation in ventricle-ablated hearts at 48 hpt (7 dpf) when compared to (B, M) CM proliferation in control ventricle-ablated (no dnMAML) hearts.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend and shown in Figure 1A-E with quantitation.

claim: Endocardial-specific dnMAML Notch inhibition prevents cardiomyocytes from proliferating in injured hearts.
source: Confocal microscopy imaging of heat-shocked/HS (A, B, L, M) vmhc:mCherry-NTR, (C, D) vmhc:mCherry-NTR; hsp70l:dnM and (N, O) vmhc:mCherry-NTR; kdrl:Cre; hsp70l:RS-dnM hearts reveals that (D) global or (O) endocardial-specific dnMAML (dnM) Notch inhibition inhibits CM proliferation in ventricle-ablated hearts at 48 hpt (7 dpf) when compared to (B, M) CM proliferation in control ventricle-ablated (no dnMAML) hearts.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend and shown in Figure 1L-P with quantitation.

claim: Global Notch inhibition between 0 and 1 dpt leads to the greatest inhibitory effect on overall recovery from ventricle injury.
source: Quantitation of the percentage of heat-shocked vmhc:mCherry-NTR, vmhc:mCherry-NTR; hsp70l:dnM and vmhc:mCherry-NTR; kdrl:Cre; hsp70l:RS-dnM ventricle-ablated hearts that display recovered ventricular tissue and contractility (black bars) at 96 hpt (nine dpf) shows that (F) global or (Q) endocardial-specific Notch inhibition between 0 and 1 dpt leads to the greatest inhibitory effect on overall recovery from ventricle injury.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend and shown in Figure 1F with quantitation.

claim: Endocardial-specific Notch inhibition between 0 and 1 dpt leads to the greatest inhibitory effect on overall recovery from ventricle injury.
source: Quantitation of the percentage of heat-shocked vmhc:mCherry-NTR, vmhc:mCherry-NTR; hsp70l:dnM and vmhc:mCherry-NTR; kdrl:Cre; hsp70l:RS-dnM ventricle-ablated hearts that display recovered ventricular tissue and contractility (black bars) at 96 hpt (nine dpf) shows that (F) global or (Q) endocardial-specific Notch inhibition between 0 and 1 dpt leads to the greatest inhibitory effect on overall recovery from ventricle injury.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend and shown in Figure 1Q with quantitation.

claim: Heat-shock induction of dnMAML-GFP inhibits the ability of genetically labeled atrial cardiomyocytes to contribute to the regeneration of ventricle-ablated hearts.
source: Confocal microscopy imaging at 72 hpt (8 dpf) reveals that (J) heat-shock induction of dnM inhibited the ability of genetically labeled c-aYFP+ atrial CMs to contribute to the regeneration of ventricle-ablated hearts when compared to (H) heat-shock control ventricle-ablated hearts.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend and shown in Figure 1G-K with quantitation.

claim: dnMAML Notch inhibition prevents atrial cardiomyocytes from regenerating the injured ventricle.
source: Quantitation of the percentage of ventricular area covered with c-aYFP+ CMs supports that dnMAML Notch inhibition prevents atrial CMs from regenerating the injured ventricle (n = 8 hsp70:dnM-, seven hsp70l:dnM+).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend and shown in Figure 1K with quantitation.

claim: Endocardial-specific dnMAML expression decreases gata4, hand2 and nkx2.5 reactivation in ventricle-ablated hearts.
source: Whole-mount in situ hybridizations of heat-shocked (P, Q, T, U, X, Y) vmhc:mCherry-NTR or (R, S, V, W, Z, Z') vmhc:mCherry-NTR; kdrl:Cre; hsp70l:RS-dnM hearts show that endocardial expression of dnM decreases (S) gata4 (n = 2/16), (W) hand2 (n = 0/5) and (Z') nkx2.5 (n = 1/7) reactivation in ventricle-ablated hearts at 48 hpt (7 dpf) when compared to (Q, U, Y) control ventricle-ablated (no dnM) hearts (n = 16/18, gata4; n = 8/8, hand2; n = 10/10, nkx2.5).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1—figure supplement 4 legend and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4P-Z'.

claim: vmhc:mCherry-NTR ventricle-ablated hearts display retrograde blood flow from the ventricle to the atrium during atrial diastole and ventricular systole.
source: In contrast to uninjured hearts which exhibit forward blood flow from atrium to ventricle throughout the cardiac cycle (Figure 2A,C, Figure 2—video 1 and Figure 2—video 3), we discovered that vmhc:mCherry-NTR ventricle-ablated hearts at 24 hpt display retrograde blood flow from the ventricle to the atrium during atrial diastole and ventricular systole (Figure 2B,D, Figure 2—video 2 and Figure 2—video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by PIV analysis shown in Figure 2A-D and videos.

claim: Altered blood flow in injured hearts results in oscillatory fluctuations of positive (anterograde) and negative (retrograde) intracardiac flow.
source: Additional PIV analyses measuring blood flow velocity within various representative regions of these hearts revealed that this altered blood flow in injured hearts results in oscillatory fluctuations of positive (anterograde) and negative (retrograde) intracardiac flow (Figure 2D–D''').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by PIV analysis shown in Figure 2D-D'''.

claim: Oscillatory blood flow is significantly increased throughout the atrium, AVC and ventricle in ventricle-ablated hearts compared to uninjured control hearts.
source: Through calculating the fundamental harmonic index (FHI = Q1/Q0, where Q1 is the amplitude of the fundamental frequency flow harmonic and Q0, the time-averaged flow) (Heckel et al., 2015) of blood flow within the atrium, AVC and ventricle, we further quantitated and confirmed that oscillatory blood flow is significantly increased throughout these regions in ventricle-ablated hearts when compared to similar regions in uninjured control hearts (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by FHI quantitation shown in Figure 2E.

claim: klf2a expression is expanded in injured hearts and present in both the AVC and the surrounding ventricular and atrial regions.
source: In situ hybridizations revealed that klf2a expression, which primarily is located in specific regions of the AVC of uninjured hearts (Figure 2F), is expanded in injured hearts and present in both the AVC and the surrounding ventricular and atrial regions (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 2F,G.

claim: klf2a:H2B-GFP expression is increased in areas of the heart exhibiting increased oscillatory flow including the AVC and its surrounding regions.
source: Using the Tg(klf2a:H2B-GFP) line, which expresses nuclear-GFP in response to changes in hemodynamic flow/stress (Heckel et al., 2015), we not only confirmed these findings (Figure 2H–J) but also created a heat-map showing that klf2a:H2B-GFP expression is increased in those areas of the heart exhibiting increased oscillatory flow including the AVC and its surrounding regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by klf2a:H2B-GFP imaging data in Figure 2H-J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: klf2a:H2B-GFP signal overlaps with Tp1:d2GFP Notch reporter activity in ablated and control hearts.
source: Furthermore, this klf2a:H2B-GFP signal overlaps with Tp1:d2GFP Notch reporter activity in ablated (and control) hearts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that these signals may be modulated by blood flow dynamics.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nearly all endocardial Tp1:nls-mCherry+ cells in injured hearts co-express the klf2a:H2B-GFP reporter.
source: Supporting that Klf2a may regulate Notch receptor expression and/or activity in response to hemodynamic flow changes as previously suggested during valve morphogenesis in zebrafish (Vermot et al., 2009), we further observed that nearly all endocardial Tp1:nls-mCherry+ cells in these hearts co-express the klf2a:H2B-GFP reporter (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by co-localization data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment reduces klf2a:H2B-GFP activity at the AVC of uninjured hearts.
source: Under each condition, we observed that klf2a:H2B-GFP activity is reduced at the AVC of uninjured hearts as previously reported (Heckel et al., 2015) (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Tricaine treatment reduces klf2a:H2B-GFP activity at the AVC of uninjured hearts.
source: Under each condition, we observed that klf2a:H2B-GFP activity is reduced at the AVC of uninjured hearts as previously reported (Heckel et al., 2015) (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: gata2a mutants reduce klf2a:H2B-GFP activity at the AVC of uninjured hearts.
source: Under each condition, we observed that klf2a:H2B-GFP activity is reduced at the AVC of uninjured hearts as previously reported (Heckel et al., 2015) (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Blebbistatin, tricaine, and gata2a mutant conditions reduce the activation of klf2a:H2B-GFP and klf2a expression throughout ventricle-injured hearts.
source: Similarly, these conditions also reduce the activation of klf2a:H2B-GFP and klf2a expression throughout ventricle-injured hearts (Figure 3A–I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by imaging and in situ hybridization data in Figure 3A-I.

claim: Tp1:d2GFP Notch reporter activity and notch1b expression are hemodynamic-sensitive in both uninjured and ventricle-ablated hearts.
source: In line with these results, we further observed that Tp1:d2GFP Notch reporter activity and notch1b expression is also hemodynamic-sensitive in both uninjured (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–L) and ventricle-ablated hearts (Figure 3J–R).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by imaging and in situ hybridization data in Figure 3J-R and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-L.

claim: Klf2a and Notch reporter and gene expression are significantly reduced after blocking contractility with blebbistatin or tricaine.
source: Although Klf2a and Notch reporter and gene expression are significantly reduced after blocking contractility with blebbistatin or tricaine, we observed that they are less affected in gata2a mutants (Figure 3E,N).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantitation in Figure 3E,N.

claim: Klf2a and Notch reporter and gene expression are less affected in gata2a mutants compared to blebbistatin or tricaine treatment.
source: Although Klf2a and Notch reporter and gene expression are significantly reduced after blocking contractility with blebbistatin or tricaine, we observed that they are less affected in gata2a mutants (Figure 3E,N).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantitation in Figure 3E,N.

claim: Ventricle-ablated hearts display reduced activation of gata4, hand2 and nkx2.5 under conditions of altered hemodynamic stress.
source: For each condition, ventricle-ablated hearts display reduced activation of the early cardiac transcription factors gata4, hand2 and nkx2.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) as well as decreased CM proliferation (Figure 4A–E), which significantly impair overall recovery from ventricular injury (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ventricle-ablated hearts display decreased cardiomyocyte proliferation under conditions of altered hemodynamic stress.
source: For each condition, ventricle-ablated hearts display reduced activation of the early cardiac transcription factors gata4, hand2 and nkx2.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) as well as decreased CM proliferation (Figure 4A–E), which significantly impair overall recovery from ventricular injury (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by proliferation quantitation in Figure 4A-E.

claim: Altered hemodynamic stress significantly impairs overall recovery from ventricular injury.
source: For each condition, ventricle-ablated hearts display reduced activation of the early cardiac transcription factors gata4, hand2 and nkx2.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) as well as decreased CM proliferation (Figure 4A–E), which significantly impair overall recovery from ventricular injury (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by recovery quantitation in Figure 4F.

claim: Reducing blood flow and viscosity significantly reduces the contribution of genetically labeled atrial cardiomyocytes to the ventricle after ventricle ablation.
source: Using a combination of Tg(amhc:CreERT2) and Tg(β-actin2:loxP-DsRed-STOP-loxP-eGFP) [or Tg(β-actin2:RSG)] lines to genetically label atrial CMs (c-aGFP+), we also discovered that reducing blood flow and viscosity under these conditions significantly reduces the contribution of c-aGFP+ labeled atrial CMs to the ventricle after ventricle ablation (Figure 4G–K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lineage tracing data in Figure 4G-K.

claim: trpv4 mutants do not exhibit retrograde blood flow.
source: Consistent with recent studies suggesting that Trpv4 controls klf2a expression (Heckel et al., 2015), we observed that trpv4 mutants, which do not exhibit retrograde blood flow (Figure 5—videos 1, 2), display reduced klf2a:H2B-GFP expression in not only uninjured (control) but also ventricle-ablated hearts (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by video data in Figure 5—videos 1, 2.

claim: trpv4 mutants display reduced klf2a:H2B-GFP expression in uninjured and ventricle-ablated hearts.
source: Consistent with recent studies suggesting that Trpv4 controls klf2a expression (Heckel et al., 2015), we observed that trpv4 mutants, which do not exhibit retrograde blood flow (Figure 5—videos 1, 2), display reduced klf2a:H2B-GFP expression in not only uninjured (control) but also ventricle-ablated hearts (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 5A-E.

claim: trpv4 and klf2a mutants display reduced Tp1:d2GFP Notch reporter and notch1b expression in uninjured and ventricle-ablated hearts.
source: Given that both trpv4 and klf2a mutants also display reduced Tp1:d2GFP Notch reporter and notch1b expression in the uninjured (control) and ventricle-ablated hearts (Figure 5F–L, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), we further examined the ability of these mutants to regenerate ablated ventricles.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by imaging and in situ hybridization data in Figure 5F-L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: klf2a and trpv4 ventricle-injured mutant hearts exhibit reduced activation of early cardiac transcription factors.
source: Similar to reducing hemodynamic blood flow and shear stress, we discovered that klf2a and trpv4 ventricle-injured mutant hearts exhibit reduced activation of early cardiac transcription factors (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) as well as diminished cardiomyocyte proliferation (Figure 5M–P), which leads to overall impaired recovery from ventricular injury (Figure 5Q).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: klf2a and trpv4 ventricle-injured mutant hearts exhibit diminished cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: Similar to reducing hemodynamic blood flow and shear stress, we discovered that klf2a and trpv4 ventricle-injured mutant hearts exhibit reduced activation of early cardiac transcription factors (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) as well as diminished cardiomyocyte proliferation (Figure 5M–P), which leads to overall impaired recovery from ventricular injury (Figure 5Q).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by proliferation quantitation in Figure 5M-P.

claim: klf2a and trpv4 mutants exhibit overall impaired recovery from ventricular injury.
source: Similar to reducing hemodynamic blood flow and shear stress, we discovered that klf2a and trpv4 ventricle-injured mutant hearts exhibit reduced activation of early cardiac transcription factors (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) as well as diminished cardiomyocyte proliferation (Figure 5M–P), which leads to overall impaired recovery from ventricular injury (Figure 5Q).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by recovery quantitation in Figure 5Q.

claim: The reprogramming of genetically labeled atrial cardiomyocytes into ventricular cardiomyocytes is significantly reduced in klf2a and trpv4 mutant hearts.
source: Corroborating these findings, lineage tracing studies further reveal that the reprogramming of genetically labeled c-aGFP+ atrial CMs into ventricular CMs to regenerate the ventricle is significantly reduced in klf2a and trpv4 mutant hearts when compared to wild-type control hearts (Figure 5R–U).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lineage tracing data in Figure 5R-U.

claim: Blocking BMP signaling with Dorsomorphin diminishes ventricle injury-induced cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: Consistent with previous cardiac regeneration studies (D'Uva et al., 2015; Gemberling et al., 2015; Mahmoud et al., 2015; Polizzotti et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2016; Xiang et al., 2016), we discovered that blocking either BMP signaling with Dorsomorphin (DM) or Erbb2 signaling with AG1478 as previously described (Han et al., 2016), diminishes not only ventricle injury-induced CM proliferation (Figure 6A–C,E) and activation of early cardiac transcription factors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), but also the trans-differentiation of genetically labeled c-aGFP+ atrial CMs into ventricular CMs (Figure 6F–H,J) when compared to DMSO controls.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by proliferation data in Figure 6A-C,E.

claim: Blocking Erbb2 signaling with AG1478 diminishes ventricle injury-induced cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: Consistent with previous cardiac regeneration studies (D'Uva et al., 2015; Gemberling et al., 2015; Mahmoud et al., 2015; Polizzotti et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2016; Xiang et al., 2016), we discovered that blocking either BMP signaling with Dorsomorphin (DM) or Erbb2 signaling with AG1478 as previously described (Han et al., 2016), diminishes not only ventricle injury-induced CM proliferation (Figure 6A–C,E) and activation of early cardiac transcription factors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), but also the trans-differentiation of genetically labeled c-aGFP+ atrial CMs into ventricular CMs (Figure 6F–H,J) when compared to DMSO controls.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by proliferation data in Figure 6A-C,E.

claim: Blocking BMP or Erbb2 signaling diminishes activation of early cardiac transcription factors after ventricular injury.
source: Consistent with previous cardiac regeneration studies (D'Uva et al., 2015; Gemberling et al., 2015; Mahmoud et al., 2015; Polizzotti et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2016; Xiang et al., 2016), we discovered that blocking either BMP signaling with Dorsomorphin (DM) or Erbb2 signaling with AG1478 as previously described (Han et al., 2016), diminishes not only ventricle injury-induced CM proliferation (Figure 6A–C,E) and activation of early cardiac transcription factors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), but also the trans-differentiation of genetically labeled c-aGFP+ atrial CMs into ventricular CMs (Figure 6F–H,J) when compared to DMSO controls.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blocking BMP or Erbb2 signaling diminishes the trans-differentiation of genetically labeled atrial cardiomyocytes into ventricular cardiomyocytes.
source: Consistent with previous cardiac regeneration studies (D'Uva et al., 2015; Gemberling et al., 2015; Mahmoud et al., 2015; Polizzotti et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2016; Xiang et al., 2016), we discovered that blocking either BMP signaling with Dorsomorphin (DM) or Erbb2 signaling with AG1478 as previously described (Han et al., 2016), diminishes not only ventricle injury-induced CM proliferation (Figure 6A–C,E) and activation of early cardiac transcription factors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), but also the trans-differentiation of genetically labeled c-aGFP+ atrial CMs into ventricular CMs (Figure 6F–H,J) when compared to DMSO controls.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lineage tracing data in Figure 6F-H,J.

claim: erbb2-/- mutants exhibit similar injury-response defects compared to AG1478-treated hearts.
source: Confirming these results, we furthermore observed that erbb2-/- mutants exhibit similar injury-response defects compared to those observed in AG1478-treated hearts (Figure 6D,E,I,J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6D,E,I,J.

claim: Inhibition of cardiomyocyte proliferation and reprogramming results in failure to regenerate the injured heart and recover from ventricle ablation.
source: As a result, this inhibition of CM proliferation and reprogramming results in the failure to regenerate the injured heart and recover from ventricle ablation (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by recovery quantitation in Figure 6K.

claim: Blocking hemodynamic flow or Notch signaling decreases the activation of myocardial BMP signaling after ventricle ablation.
source: Using the Tg(BRE:d2GFP) BMP reporter line, which has been previously used to detect BMP signaling in the myocardium of zebrafish hearts (Han et al., 2016), we observed that blocking either hemodynamic flow or Notch signaling decreases the activation of myocardial BMP signaling that occurs after ventricle ablation (Figure 7A–F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by BRE:d2GFP reporter data in Figure 7A-F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: bmp10 and nrg1 expression are elevated in the heart after ventricle injury.
source: We found by in situ hybridization analyses that while the expression of these factors are elevated in the heart after ventricle injury, this increased expression is blocked after inhibiting hemodynamic flow and Notch signaling (Figure 7G–R, Figure 7—figure supplement 2), suggesting that these ligands may also regulate BMP and Erbb2 during CM reprogramming and cardiac regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7G-R.

claim: Increased bmp10 and nrg1 expression after ventricle injury is blocked after inhibiting hemodynamic flow and Notch signaling.
source: We found by in situ hybridization analyses that while the expression of these factors are elevated in the heart after ventricle injury, this increased expression is blocked after inhibiting hemodynamic flow and Notch signaling (Figure 7G–R, Figure 7—figure supplement 2), suggesting that these ligands may also regulate BMP and Erbb2 during CM reprogramming and cardiac regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7G-R and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: bmp10 and nrg1 may regulate BMP and Erbb2 during cardiomyocyte reprogramming and cardiac regeneration.
source: We found by in situ hybridization analyses that while the expression of these factors are elevated in the heart after ventricle injury, this increased expression is blocked after inhibiting hemodynamic flow and Notch signaling (Figure 7G–R, Figure 7—figure supplement 2), suggesting that these ligands may also regulate BMP and Erbb2 during CM reprogramming and cardiac regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a suggestion based on the expression data.

claim: Hemodynamic-mediated endocardial signaling pathways may regulate cardiomyocyte reprogramming and heart regeneration through modulating myocardial BMP and Erbb2 signaling.
source: Altogether, these findings support that hemodynamic-mediated endocardial signaling pathways may regulate CM reprogramming and heart regeneration through modulating myocardial BMP and Erbb2 signaling.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings presented in the results section.

claim: Near complete ablation of the entire heart using a cmlc2:NTR-based system may result in significantly reduced heart recovery and fish survival compared to ventricular-specific ablation.
source: Furthermore, our results may explain why near complete ablation/injury of the entire heart (i.e. both atrial and ventricular chambers) using a cmlc2:NTR-based system (Curado et al., 2007) may result in significantly reduced heart recovery and fish survival compared to our studies as these hearts may exhibit overall weaker beating and reduced oscillatory flow compared to those where ventricular cardiomyocytes are specifically ablated but atrial cardiomyocytes are spared (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings with citations.

claim: Inflammatory and hypoxia pathways have been suggested to activate repair responses during heart regeneration.
source: Although inflammatory and hypoxia pathways have been suggested to activate repair responses during heart regeneration (Fang et al., 2013; Jopling et al., 2012; Nakada et al., 2017), we discovered that the injured heart is also able to sense altered intracardiac hemodynamic forces through the endocardial biomechanical sensor Trpv4, thereby activating an endocardial-myocardial signaling pathway that directs cardiomyocyte reprogramming and heart repair.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: The injured heart is able to sense altered intracardiac hemodynamic forces through the endocardial biomechanical sensor Trpv4.
source: Although inflammatory and hypoxia pathways have been suggested to activate repair responses during heart regeneration (Fang et al., 2013; Jopling et al., 2012; Nakada et al., 2017), we discovered that the injured heart is also able to sense altered intracardiac hemodynamic forces through the endocardial biomechanical sensor Trpv4, thereby activating an endocardial-myocardial signaling pathway that directs cardiomyocyte reprogramming and heart repair.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Trpv4 can transduce hemodynamic forces through Klf2 to activate endocardial Notch signaling during cardiac regeneration.
source: Similar to biomechanical signaling mechanisms deployed during cardiac development (Heckel et al., 2015), Trpv4 can transduce these forces through Klf2 to activate endocardial Notch signaling, which has been recently reported to be crucial for regulating adult zebrafish heart regeneration (Münch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: Endocardial Notch signaling is crucial for regulating adult zebrafish heart regeneration.
source: Similar to biomechanical signaling mechanisms deployed during cardiac development (Heckel et al., 2015), Trpv4 can transduce these forces through Klf2 to activate endocardial Notch signaling, which has been recently reported to be crucial for regulating adult zebrafish heart regeneration (Münch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Münch et al., 2017.

claim: Endocardial Notch signaling may act non-cell autonomously to promote cardiac reprogramming and repair through modulating myocardial BMP and Erbb2 signaling pathways.
source: In addition to its potential role in regulating inflammatory responses (Münch et al., 2017), we discovered that this endocardial Notch signaling may act non-cell autonomously to promote cardiac reprogramming and repair through modulating both myocardial BMP and Erbb2 signaling pathways, thus further illuminating how injury-activated endocardium may mediate myocardial regeneration as previously suggested (Kikuchi et al., 2011; Münch et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: This hemodynamic-mediated cardiac repair signaling mechanism may participate in regulating adaptive cardiac responses during mammalian cardiac injury.
source: Given the role of BMP and Erbb2 signaling in not only zebrafish but also mammalian adult heart regeneration (D'Uva et al., 2015; Gemberling et al., 2015; Mahmoud et al., 2015; Polizzotti et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2016; Xiang et al., 2016), our results raise the possibility that this hemodynamic-mediated cardiac repair signaling mechanism may also participate in regulating adaptive cardiac responses during mammalian cardiac injury.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation based on the findings and citations.

claim: Biomechanical forces may impact mammalian heart regeneration through modulating BMP and Erbb2 signaling pathways and interacting with other injury-response mechanisms including hypoxia and inflammation.
source: Thus, future studies are warranted in mammalian model systems including the mouse to explore whether and how hemodynamic forces may impact mammalian heart regeneration through not only modulating BMP and Erbb2 signaling pathways but also interacting with other injury-response mechanisms including hypoxia and inflammation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion for future research.
